entities.name: Achard of Saint-Victor
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Achard of Saint-Victor (c. 1100–1171) was a French theologian, canon regular of the Abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, and eventually Bishop of Avranches in Normandy. As a Victorine — the school of mystical and speculative theology founded at Saint-Victor by William of Champeaux and developed by Hugh and Richard of Saint-Victor — he was part of one of the twelfth century's most creative theological movements.

The School of Saint-Victor was the pre-eminent intellectual centre of twelfth-century Paris, pioneering the integration of monastic contemplation with rigorous scholastic method. Achard's theological works — including his treatise 'De unitate Dei et pluralitate creaturarum' (On the Unity of God and the Plurality of Creatures) — engaged the central metaphysical questions of Trinitarian theology and creation with both speculative rigour and mystical depth. His work synthesised Neoplatonic theology with Christian Trinitarian doctrine in ways that influenced later Scholasticism.

His appointment as Bishop of Avranches (1161) took him out of the Parisian intellectual environment into the pastoral and administrative demands of a Norman diocese. His career exemplifies the pattern of twelfth-century scholar-bishops who combined the new university-related learning with episcopal governance. His works remained in manuscript circulation and were rediscovered by twentieth-century medieval scholars as significant witnesses to Victorine speculative theology.
